claims.text: The as-received AlCrFeNiSi powder has a particle-size distribution suitable for binder jetting and subsequent sintering.
Approximately 1100–1200 °C is an applicable sintering window for binder-jetted AlCrFeNiSi.
AlCrFeNiSi should be sintered in an inert or vacuum environment.
A sintering hold of 2–4 hours is appropriate for the proposed process.
Uniform heating and slow cooling will minimize internal stress in the sintered parts.
The proposed process is applicable to miniature components less than 10 mm thick.
Binder jetting followed by isothermal sintering produces lower thermal gradients than laser- or electron-beam fusion processes.
Post-print sintering causes less microstructural coarsening than rapid fusion-based processing.
Large thermal gradients generated by rapid fusion processing cause residual-stress buildup and cracking.
Controlled isothermal sintering promotes diffusion-driven densification and interdiffusion.
Controlled sintering promotes formation of a structurally homogeneous alloy.
The sintering-derived uniform microstructure will yield more consistent mechanical performance.
Binder-jetted and sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have significantly lower residual stresses than laser powder bed fused counterparts.
Binder-jetted and sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have greater microstructural homogeneity than laser powder bed fused counterparts.
Binder-jetted and sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have comparable or better strength and ductility than laser powder bed fused counterparts.
Replacing laser powder bed fusion with binder jetting and sintering will reduce production complexity.
A laser power greater than 200 W represents a typical high-thermal-load baseline for additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi.
Laser powder bed fusion involves rapid melting and solidification.
Sintering shrinkage may require design compensation to preserve net shape in miniature components.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires significantly lower residual stress, but the falsification rule only rejects results that fail to outperform or match laser powder bed fusion. Equal residual stress would count as matching and would therefore not falsify the stated significantly-lower-stress prediction.
